newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan oil statistics show big Saudi sales gains.
newsitem.headline: Japan oil statistics show big Saudi sales gains.

text.p: April's gain in Japanese crude imports may be a statistical anomaly, but a look at the first four months of 1997 as a whole shows definite winners and losers in the trade ministry's monthly tally.

Japan's crude oil imports in April rose 6.9 percent over year-earlier levels, to 22.98 million kilolitres (kl), or 4.78 million barrels-per-day (bpd), according to Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) statistics on Monday.
But MITI officials were quick to point out that the April gain was mainly a factor of shipping arrangements.
"This month there is nothing special behind the rise as it resulted largely from the timing of individual arrivals," a ministry official said.
Late arriving March deliveries, for example, were likely to have been included in the April statistics, the official said.

Year-to-date comparisons, however, show Japanese purchases of Saudi Arabian grades during the first four months of 1997 were some 17 percent higher than in the same period in 1996 and 11 percent higher than in the first four months of 1995.
"One reason is that Idemitsu increased its term volume (of Saudi Arabian crudes) from 160,000 bpd to 200,000," said one Japan trader.
Refiner Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd was not immediately available for comment.
"But in a more general sense, last winter's spot market premiums were extremely high, especially for Abu Dhabi, Qatar, and Oman grades," the trader said.

"As a result many Japanese term customers asked the Saudis to supply additional barrels, and to some extent they did." Saudi Arabian sales amounted to 5.14 million kl (1.08 million bpd) over the first four months of this year.

Meanwhile, year-to-date Oman deliveries, at 1.13 million kl (237,000 bpd), have been 12 percent lower in 1997 than in the same period in 1996 and 24 percent lower than in the first four months of 1995.
Similarly, Qatar's year-to-date exports to Japan, at 1.48 million kl (310,000 bpd), have fallen by six percent from last year and by almost seven percent from 1995.
Yemen was the biggest loser in the MITI report.

In the first four months of April, Yemeni deliveries to Japan trickled in at just 71,000 kl (15,000 bpd), an 85 percent plunge from the same period in 1996, and a 66 percent fall from the first four months of 1995.
"This occured at a point in time when the Brent/Dubai differential was wide, so Yemeni barrels were not attractive to us," said one trader.
Yemeni prices, which are related to dated Brent, are most affordable in Asia when the Brent/Dubai spread is lean.
April also featured the first Japanese imports of Thailand's Irawan condensate in at least three years.
Traders said the volume, which amounted to 64,000 kl (13,500 barrel per day), was used as a naphtha replacement in petrochemical production.

Another highlight was a 290,000 kl (60,000 bpd) volume of Iraqi crude. The purchase is the second since Japan in February picked up its first Iraq crude imports in over six years. --Tokyo Energy Desk (+813-5473-3708)
